note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — UNBRANCHED RYE SPIKE
tiles.details: Follow the central rachis on the attached flowering ear (panel 0): rye bears ONE sessile spikelet at successive alternating rachis nodes, typically with TWO fertile florets and sometimes a reduced third. Source-labelled detached rye spikelets are shown in panels 4–5, but none proves a calibrated attached node. Do not substitute an old CC BY-NC research image for the public-ready ear. Cultivated rye is introduced, not a Hays-native restoration species.
tiles.short: One narrow two-ranked terminal spike, not a loose branched oat panicle.
tiles.status: SOURCE-IDENTIFIED PHOTO — ATTACHED NODE STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED ANNUAL AND ACTUAL COLLAR
tiles.details: Inspect the actual blade–sheath junction: panel 1 shows multiple rye collar/auricle angles beside a 10-mm reference, and panel 2 shows the true membranous ligule with a photographed 3-mm scale. Published ligule ranges are approximately 0.5–1.5 mm (New Zealand cultivated rye treatment) or 1–2 mm (VicFlora); do not claim a new specimen measurement from the source scale without calibrated pixel review. Auricles may be small or obscure. Neither collar photograph establishes a connected rooted Texas plant.
tiles.short: Fibrous-rooted cool-season cereal; short 0.5–1.5 mm membranous ligule, sometimes small auricles.
tiles.status: GENUINE SCALED COLLAR/LIGULE PHOTOS INSTALLED; ROOTED SAME-PLANT VIEW STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT SPIKELETS PER RACHIS NODE
tiles.details: Examine one intact mature rachis node at 10–20×: rye has ONE usually two-flowered spikelet per node; little barley has THREE one-flowered spikelets. Panel 0 shows an attached flowering rye ear, panels 4–5 show detached rye spikelets, and panel 7 is a correctly labeled DIFFERENT-species little barley comparison. None is a same-scale, fully exposed rye-versus-barley rachis-node dissection. Wheat also has one spikelet per node but generally more florets and broader glumes.
tiles.short: Rye = ONE usually two-flowered spikelet per node; barley = THREE one-flowered spikelets.
tiles.status: DETACHED SPIKELET PHOTOS — NODE MICRO MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMAS AND DIFFERENT AWNS
tiles.details: Dissect a mature spikelet and isolate the two stiff rough-keeled glumes (NZ 7–12.5 mm; broader Flora of North America genus 8–20 mm), each with a short glume awnlet. The lemma has a comb-ciliate keel and a much longer terminal awn (NZ 15–65 mm). Do not call the glume awnlet a fertile lemma awn. Existing spikelet panels do not resolve all veins or both awn origins at a calibrated scale.
tiles.short: Two narrow one-veined glumes ~7–12.5 mm in NZ; firm five-veined lemmas ~10–20 mm.
tiles.status: SOURCE-BASED MEASUREMENTS — DISSECTION WITH SCALE MISSING

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Gallery panel 6 is Canada wildrye (Elymus canadensis), with paired spikelets; panel 7 is little barley (Hordeum pusillum), with THREE spikelets per rachis node. These are genuine other-species comparisons, not rye anatomical proof. Wild oat (Avena fatua) has a loose branched panicle with bent/twisted dorsal lemma awns. Wheat (Triticum aestivum) often has broader multi-flowered spikelets. Compare actual attached nodes, glumes and floret counts; do not rely on color or awn length alone.
tiles.short: Little barley = triple spikelets; wild oat = branched panicle; wheat/wildrye need node dissection.

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND EXACT HANDOFF
tiles.details: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS. Six rye JPEGs are physically archived: five source-licensed public-eligible views (including an attached flowering ear, two scaled collar/ligule photos and two detached spikelet photos) plus one old CC BY-NC image requiring its own public-rights decision. Eight gallery panels include two correctly labeled OTHER-species comparisons (Canada wildrye and little barley), with four existing broad markers. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: a same-voucher rooted rye with mature ear; a 1-mm calibrated intact rachis node proving one attached two-flowered spikelet; isolated one-veined glumes and their short awnlets versus five-veined comb-ciliate lemma with long terminal awn. The scaled true ligule/collar photographic role is already represented; do not duplicate it, but independently measure the free edge if claiming a numerical value. NEEDS_SITE_QA: check six archived files, eight panels, four existing arrows, individual CC BY-NC/CC BY-SA 2.0/3.0/4.0 terms, image EXIF/GPS, comparison labels and mobile public rendering. No Pages verification or microscopic arrows are claimed.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — five archived source photos; new genuine scaled collar

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: CEREAL RYE (INTRODUCED): find a fibrous-rooted cool-season cereal with one narrow unbranched, often awned terminal SPIKE, not a branched oat panicle. Follow the rachis: ONE sessile spikelet alternates at each node, usually containing TWO fertile florets (sometimes a reduced third). Under 10–20× verify two narrow one-veined awl-like glumes, and five-veined sharply keeled lemmas with rough/ciliate keels and long terminal awns. At the true leaf collar check a short MEMBRANOUS ligule and small auricles when present. Hordeum has THREE spikelets per node; wheat has broader multi-flowered spikelets; wildryes have paired spikelets. Not a Hays-native restoration grass.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: FIRST see Rasbak's source-labelled photo of an attached flowering rye ear: narrow green-blue ear with upward-pointing awns and yellow hanging pollen anthers. This is authentic reproductive architecture, not an isolated spikelet.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Inspect the actual blade–sheath junction: panel 1 shows multiple rye collar/auricle angles beside a 10-mm reference, and panel 2 shows the true membranous ligule with a photographed 3-mm scale. Published ligule ranges are approximately 0.5–1.5 mm (New Zealand cultivated rye treatment) or 1–2 mm (VicFlora); do not claim a new specimen measurement from the source scale without calibrated pixel review. Auricles may be small or obscure. Neither collar photograph establishes a connected rooted Texas plant.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Examine one intact mature rachis node at 10–20×: rye has ONE usually two-flowered spikelet per node; little barley has THREE one-flowered spikelets. Panel 0 shows an attached flowering rye ear, panels 4–5 show detached rye spikelets, and panel 7 is a correctly labeled DIFFERENT-species little barley comparison. None is a same-scale, fully exposed rye-versus-barley rachis-node dissection. Wheat also has one spikelet per node but generally more florets and broader glumes.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Little barley (Hordeum pusillum) has triple spikelets at each rachis node and a much smaller tuft, whereas Secale cereale has a large continuous spike with individual 2-flowered spikelets alternating along the axis; distinguish from wheat Triticum aestivum by bract features, glumes and cereal head morphology.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: ACTUAL FLOWERING RYE EAR — long awns and dangling yellow pollen anthers (Rasbak)
panels.caption: Rasbak's photograph of genuinely flowering cereal rye: follow the densely arranged upright ear, pointed awns, and hanging yellow anthers. Compare the separate Matt Lavin detached spikelets and Stefan.lefnaer measured inner ligule views. These are DIFFERENT specimens—not same-plant dissections.

panels.caption: Real Secale cereale inner collar viewed at macro scale. The whitish/torn-looking membrane clasping the culm is the short TRUE ligule. Do not confuse it with the curved sheath margin. The photographer includes a 3 mm scale bar.

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE — CANADA WILDRYE (not cereal rye): paired spikelets on arching wild head
panels.caption: COMPARE ANOTHER GRASS: Canada wildrye, Elymus canadensis, arches or nods when mature, with outward-spreading awns. Our real rye photo earlier is a straight narrow flowering ear with exposed yellow anthers. Never infer identification from awns alone.
panels.creator: Matt Lavin

panels.label: LOOK-ALIKE — LITTLE BARLEY (not cereal rye): compact erect awned flowering spike
panels.caption: COMPARE ANOTHER GRASS: Little barley, Hordeum pusillum, has a compact erect awned flowering head. Though cereal rye can also be awned and upright, the arrangement of multiple barley spikelets differs under a hand lens. This is actual little barley, not another rye photo.

memory_rule: CEREAL RYE is a cultivated/escaped INTRODUCED cool-season cereal grass with long narrow terminal spikes and rows of overlapping spikelets bearing long awns; each spikelet usually has two fertile florets. Contrast with Hordeum pusillum: true barley makes triads of 3 spikelets at rachis nodes. Rye is not a Hays-native restoration grass.
safety_note: Six physically archived rye photos, five public eligible and one CC BY-NC held. Real inner ligule and four collar views with rulers ARE installed; these were missing only in old lesson wording. Attached actual flowering ear now present, but rooted whole plant and wheat matched-scale comparison absent; real Canada wildrye and little barley other-species photos added without identical scale. Same-specimen dissected glume/lemma/original scale still unverified; mobile photo-arrow and site QA outstanding.
field_rule: Pair a true attached rye ear with the measured true inner ligule and real detached large florets; compare entire mature rye spikelets to wheat, barley and wildrye before confirming from awns alone.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
